Rectifier. A circuit that converts alternating current into direct current using one or more diodes to allow current flow in only one direction. Rectifiers form the front end of nearly all DC power supplies, converting utility AC at fifty to sixty hertz or transformer-secondary AC into a rough but usable DC voltage.

A half-wave rectifier uses a single diode to block the negative half-cycle. Only half the AC input appears at the output, resulting in fifty percent efficiency and high ripple. A full-wave rectifier uses two diodes and a center-tapped transformer to reverse the negative half-cycle, delivering twice the power of half-wave and lower ripple.

A bridge rectifier, also called a Graetz bridge, uses four diodes arranged so that regardless of AC polarity, current flows in the same direction. This is the most common topology and requires no center tap. The output of any rectifier is pulsating direct current. The ripple voltage, which is the AC component, decays as one divided by the product of frequency and filter capacitor. A larger capacitor reduces ripple.

Peak inverse voltage is the maximum reverse voltage across a diode during the non-conducting half-cycle. The diode rating must exceed peak inverse voltage to prevent breakdown. A safety margin of roughly two times is recommended. A rectifier diode like the 1N4007 has fast switching speed and high voltage and current ratings. Slower, cheaper options suffice if the frequency is low.

The direct current average of a full-wave rectified sine is approximately zero point six three six times the peak voltage, or zero point four five times the RMS voltage. This is the nominal output before filtering. Synchronous rectification uses MOSFETs instead of diodes to reduce forward-drop losses in high-current supplies. This is critical in battery chargers and DC-to-DC converters.
